# Correction: Systems analysis of the CO2 concentrating mechanism in cyanobacteria ## Authors - Niall M Mangan † - Michael P Brenner † Corresponding author ## Table 2. Enzymatic rates We recalculated the enzymatic rates for carbonic anhydrase and RuBisCO. The values for Vmax and K1/2 listed in the previous version of Table 2 used the incorrect 6.022 × 1022 value for Avogadro's number. All plots in the original paper were for those values. All new plots are for the values listed in the updated table, using Avogadro's number 6.022 × 1023. The Vmax values are all about an order of magnitude lower than previously calculated.

## Figure 2. Phase space for HCO3− transport and carboxysome permeability The main effect of correcting Avagadro's number is that the peak defining optimal carboxysome permeability is lower and broader. The optimal carboxhysome permeability for a target carboxysomal CO2 concentration is found by looking at the leftmost value on a line of constant concentration on the permeability vs HCO3− transport plot. This point represents the carboxysome permeability where the least amount of HCO3− transport is needed to achieve a given carboxysomal CO2 concentration. For 99% carboxylation (cyan curve below) this value is now around kc = 10−3 cm/s (previously kc = 6 × 10−3 cm/s). Carbonic anhydrase also saturates at a lower HCO3− transport value. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** The leftmost line (dark blue) indicates for what values of jc and kc the CO2 concentration in the carboxysome would half-saturate RuBisCO (Km). The middle line (light blue) indicates the parameter values which would result in a CO2 concentration where 99% of all RuBisCO reactions are carboxylation reactions and only 1% are oxygenation reactions when O2 concentration is 260 μM. To the left of the line the error is greater and to the right it is smaller. The right most (red) line indicates the parameter values which result in carbonic anhydrase saturating. Here the rate of conversion from CO2 to $HCO_{3}^{−}$, α = 0, so there is no CO2 scavenging or facilitated uptake of CO2. The dotted line (grey) shows the kc and jc values, where the $HCO_{3}^{−}$ concentration in the cytosol is 30 mM. The $HCO_{3}^{−}$ concentration in the cytosol does not vary appreciably with kc in this parameter regime, and reaches 30 mM at $j_{c}≈0.6 cm/s$. All other parameters, such as reaction rates are held fixed and the values can be found in the Tables 1 and 2. ## Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Effect of decreased diffusion in the carboxysome With the correction, decreasing the diffusion constant in the carboxysome has much less of an effect on the phase space plot. For optimal or larger carboxysome permeability, there is very little effect (kc ≥ 10−3 cm/s). ![Figure 2—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2—figure supplement 1.:** Phase space for $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport and carboxysome permeability for varying diffusion in the carboxysome.Solid lines show lines of constant CO2 concentration in the carboxysome for $D_{c}=1\times10^{−5} \frac{cm^{2}}{s}$, or the diffusion constant of small molecule in water. Dashed lines show the same lines of constant CO2 concentration, bur for $D_{c}=1\times10^{−7} \frac{cm^{2}}{s}$, or the diffusion constant of a small molecule in a 60% sucrose solution. ## Figure 2—figure supplement 2. Effect of CO2 scavenging or facilitated uptake The correction reduces the effect of facilitated uptake. At the optimal permeability it has nearly no effect (difference between dashed and solid lines near kc = 10−3 cm/s). ![Figure 2—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 2—figure supplement 2.:** Effect of CO2 scavenging or facilitated uptake on phase space for $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport, jc, and carboxysome permeability, kc.Plotted are the parameter values at which CO2 concentration reaches some critical value. The leftmost line (dark blue) indicates for what values of jc and kc the CO2 concentration in the carboxysome would saturate RuBisCO. The middle line (light blue) indicates the parameter values which would result in a CO2 concentration where 99% of all RuBisCO reactions are carboxylation reactions and only 1% are oxygenation reactions when O2 concentration is 260 μM. The rightmost (red) line indicates the parameter values which result in carbonic anhydrase saturating. Here α = 0 cm/s (solid lines) and α = 1 cm/s (dashed line), showing the effect of CO2 scavenging or facilitated uptake on the phase space. All other parameters, such as reaction rates are held fixed and the values can be found Table 1. ## Figure 3. CO2 concentration in the carboxysome as function of HCO3− transport: comparison of numeric and analytic solutions We plot Figure 3 assuming the new optimal carboxysome permeability of kc = 10−3 cm/s (previously kc = 6 × 10−3 cm/s). There is very little change from the previous Figure 3, with the updated carboxysome permeability. Had we plotted at the same kc = 6 × 10−3 cm/s, the CO2 would have been lower, because the system would not be at the optimal permeability. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig4-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport is varied, and all other system parameters are held constant. The CO2 concentration above which RuBisCO is saturated is Km (grey dashed line). The CO2 concentration where the oxygen reaction error rate will be 1% is C99% (grey dash-dotted line). The transition between carbonic anhydrase being unsaturated and saturated happens where the two analytic solutions meet (where the dashed and solid red lines meet). Below a critical value of transport, $j_{c}≈10^{−3} cm/s$ the level of transport is lower than the $HCO_{3}^{−}$ leaking through the cell membrane. For these simulations and solutions the carboxysome permeability was kc = 10−3 cm/s (in previous version kc = 6 × 10−3 cm/s was used). ## Figure 3—figure supplement 1. No effect of localizing carbonic anhydrase to the shell of the carboxysome The correction did not at all effect the conclusion that the organization of carbonic anhydrase within the carboxysome has no effect on the resulting concentrations. Consistent with updated Figure 2—figure supplement 1, the effect of decreasing the diffusion in carboxysome is much less prominent than in the original manuscript. ![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig5-v1.jpg) **Figure 3—figure supplement 1.:** We assume the same amount of carbonic anhydrase and RuBisCO activity for each simulation and compare the case with the enzymes evenly distributed throughout the carboxysome to the case where the carbonic anhydrase is localized to the inner carboxysome shell. The (-.-) lines are for no organization and (x) for organized with Dc = 10−5 cm2/s. The (…) lines are for no organization and (o) are for organized with Dc = 10−5 cm2/s. ## Figure 4. CO2 concentration in the carboxysome with varying carboxysome permeability The correction does not effect the conclusion that an optimal carboxysome permeability exists, or what causes it, but it changes its absolute value. The correction has two main effects: (1) it decreases the optimal carboxysome permeability (seen as a shift in the peak) by a factor of 6, and (2) for carboxysome permeabilities higher than optimal (kc > 0.1 cm/s) the CO2 concentration is an order of magnitude lower. Therefore the optimal carboxysome permeability peak is at a lower kc value and more prominent. ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig6-v1.jpg) **Figure 4.:** (A) Numerical solution (diamonds and circles) and analytic solutions (carbonic anhydrase unsaturated, solid lines, and saturated, dashed lines) correspond well. On all plots CO2 (red circle) $ Formula [picomoles(cell s)] % Of flux HCO3− transport jcHout 3.26 × 10−4 HCO3− leakage kmH(Hout−Hcytosol(Rb)) 3.2 × 10−4 98.6% CO2 leakage kmC(Cout−Ccytosol(Rb)) 4.5 × 10−6 1.4% carboxylation VmaxCC+Km(1+OKO) 8.2 × 10−8 0.03% oxygenation VmaxOCC+KmO(1+CKC) 6.7 × 10−10 2 × 10−4 % ## Table 4. ## Discussion of fluxes and resulting 2-phosphoglycolate, and 3-phosphoglycerate production The discussion of the number of transporters needed for this magnitude of $HCO_{3}^{−}$ influx increases by an order of magnitude from $10^{3} \frac{transporters}{\mum^{2}}$ to $10^{4} \frac{transporters}{\mum^{2}}$. While the change in uptake is less than a factor of two different, the conversion from picomoles/s to molecules/s for a cell used the incorrect value of Avogadro's number. So this is now about an order of magnitude larger than the number of ATP synthase complexes on the thylakoid membrane of spinach. The numbers for net flux of $HCO_{3}−$ change slightly. For jc = 0.6 cm/s the net flux is $6\times10^{−6}\frac{pmol}{cell s}$ compared to the previous value of $10^{−5}\frac{pmol}{cell s}$ and for jc = 0.06 cm/s the net flux is $9\times10^{−7} \frac{pmol}{cell s}$ compared with the previous value of $1\times10^{−6} \frac{pmol}{cell s}$. So the conclusion that measured net fluxes of $10^{−6}\frac{pmol}{cell s}$ compares best with the lower $HCO_{3}^{−}$ flux still holds. Since Avagadro's number effects the rate of carboxylation and oxygenation, the recalculated values for 2-phosphoglycolate and 3-phosphoglycerate production are lower. This exacerbates the large amount of energy that appears to go into CO2 concentration compared to the actual fixation. Now around 0.03% of concentrated inorganic carbon is fixed into 3-phosphoglycerate. Over 99.9% is lost to leakage either in the form of CO2 or $HCO_{3}^{−}$ (previously these values were calculated to be 99%). The higher $HCO_{3}^{−}$ flux assumption (Table 3) predicts that only 217 2-phosphoglycolate are produced a second, and the lower $HCO_{3}^{−}$ flux assumption (Table 4) predicts that 1.4 × 103 2-phosphoglycolate are produced a second. So the higher flux allows the production of many fewer 2-phosphoglycolate than previously estimated. Recalculating the time to fix the necessary carbon to replicate a cell results in 7–21 hr for the higher flux rate (Table 3) and 11–35 hr for the lower flux rate (Table 4). Both are consistant with the division times of cyanobacteria, but the higher flux rate is a better match. In conclusion, the correction further highlights the puzzle of how much energy cyanobacteria must use $HCO_{3}^{−}$ to achieve a level of CO2 which creates adequate fixation rates. Either cyanobacteria use a much larger amount of energy to achieve this internal concentration than to fix each CO2, the permeability of the cell must be much lower for $HCO_{3}^{−}$ than assumed here, or there is another mechanism not covered in this model. ## Figure 5. Flux of HCO3− from varying sources as the proportion of CO2 to HCO3− outside the cell changes The correction decreases the effect of CO2 scavenging at high permeabilities (kc = 1 cm/s and 10−2 cm/s). It now appears to be negligible compared to HOC3− uptake and CO2 uptake for all permeabilities. Only when CO2 concentration is a very small percentage of the external carbon, does the scavenging contribute more than the CO2 uptake, and both are far less than HCO3− uptake. ![Figure 5.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig7-v1.jpg) **Figure 5.:** Size of the $HCO_{3}^{−}$ flux in one cell from varying sources, as the proportion of CO2 to $HCO_{3}^{−}$ outside the cell changes changes.We show results for three carboxysome permeabilities, kc, and only the scavenging is effected. Total external inorganic carbon is 15 μM, jc = 1 cm/s and $\frac{\alpha}{K_{\alpha}}=1 cm/s$. Scavenging is negligibly small for all values of kc shown. Unless there is very little $HCO_{3}^{−}$ in the environment, $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport seems to be more efficient than CO2 facilitated uptake. ## Figure 6. CO2 concentration with various organizations of enzymes in the cell With the corrected Avagadro's number the CO2 concentration is significantly lower in all but the optimal permeability case, making the error rate drastically higher. The effect of optimal permeability on CO2 concentration is, therefore, much larger. ![Figure 6.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06400/elife-06400-fig8-v1.jpg) **Figure 6.:** Concentration of CO2 achieved through various cellular organizations of enzymes, where we have selected the $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport level such that the $HCO_{3}^{−}$ concentration in the cytosol is 30 mM.O2 concentration is 260 μM. The oxygenation error rates, as a percent of total RuBisCO reactions are indicated on the concentration bars. The cellular organizations investigated are RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase distributed throughout the entire cytosol, co-localizing RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase on a scaffold at the center of the cell without a carboxysome shell, RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase encapsulated in a carboxysome with high permeability at the center of the cell, and RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase encapsulated in a carboxysome with optimal permeability at the center of the cell. ## Corrections to text Throughout the text the default $HCO_{3}^{−}$ flux has been changed from $j_{c}=0.7\frac{cm}{s}$ to $j_{c}=0.6\frac{cm}{s}$ and optimal carboxysome permeability from $k_{c}=6\times10^{−3}\frac{cm}{s}$ to $k_{c}=10^{−3}\frac{cm}{s}$.In the discussion of fluxes and concentrations we previously had written: ‘Our simulated cell has a flux of 2 × 107 molecules/s. Assuming the rate of transport per transporter of $10^{3}\frac{molecules}{s}$ and our cell’s surface area this requires about $10^{3}\frac{transporters}{\mum^{2}}$. This is actually not that far off from the number of ATP synthase complexes on the thylakoid membrane in spinach, $700\frac{complexes}{\mum^{2}}$ (Miller and Staehelin, 1979), although it is still quite high.’ This is now: ‘Our simulated cell has a flux of 2 × 108molecules/s. Assuming the rate of transport per transporter of $10^{3}\frac{molecules}{s}$ and our cell’s surface area this requires about $10^{4}\frac{transporters}{\mum^{2}}$. This is about an order of magnitude higher than the number of ATP synthase complexes on the thylakoid membrane in spinach, $700\frac{complexes}{\mum^{2}}$ (Miller and Staehelin, 1979).’In the discussion of fluxes and concentrations we previously had written: ‘At the higher flux rate (Table 3) this means that a cell could replicate every 1–2 hr, so faster than cyanobacteria replicate. The lower flux rate (Table 4) would produce fix enough CO2 for the cell to replicate every 8 to 21 hr, which is similar to the division times of cyanobacteria.’ This is now: ‘At the higher flux rate (Table 3) this means that a cell could replicate every 7–21 hr and the lower flux rate (Table 4) allows replication every 11 to 35 hr. Both are consistent with the division times of cyanobacteria.’In the caption of Figure 5 we had written: ‘When the carboxysome permeability is larger than optimal, kc = 1 cm/s, scavenging can contribute more than facilitated uptake at low external CO2 concentrations. However, when the carboxysome permeability at or below our geometric bound, kc <= 0.02 cm/s, scavenging is negligibly small.’ This is now: ‘Scavenging is negligibly small for all values of kc shown.’In the text of the Benefit of CO2 to $HCO_{3}^{−}$ conversion: facilitated uptake or scavenging of CO2 we had written: ‘Scavenging only contributes significantly to total incoming $HCO_{3}^{−}$ when the carboxysome permeability is higher than optimal, Figure 5, and does not contribute significantly below our calculated upper bound of $k_{c}<=0.02cm/s$. In these ranges for carboxysome permeability, there is very little CO2 leaking out of the carboxysome into the cytosol, so there is very little CO2 to scavenge, Figure 5.’ This is now: ‘Scavenging is negligibly small for all values of kc shown. There is very little CO2 in the cytosol, so there is very little CO2 to scavenge, Figure 5.’There were also a few typos we have now corrected:In the Reaction diffusion model section we had: ‘RuBisCO also requires ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, the substrate which CO2 reacts with to produce 3-phosphoglycolate.’ This has been corrected to ‘… CO2 reacts with to produce 3-phosphoglycerate.’in Table 1: ‘$k_{m}^{H}$ permeability of cell membrane to CO2’ has been corrected to: ‘$k_{m}^{H}$ permeability of cell membrane to $HCO_{3}^{−}$’.Table 2 header said kcut which has been corrected to kcat.In the Varying $HCO_{3}^{−}$ transport saturates enzyme section we had:The chemical equilibrium is $K_{eq}=H/C=(K_{ba}V_{ca})(K_{ca}V_{ba})≈5$, for pH around 7 (DeVoe and Kistiakowsky, 1961), so that $HCO_{3}^{−}$ > CO2 in the carboxysome.The equation is now: $K_{eq}=H/C=(KbaVca)/(KcaVba)≈5$.In Figure 3—figure supplement 1 the units for Dc on both the plot and caption are cm/s, they should be cm2/s.

results.result: The original manuscript used an incorrect value for Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10^22 instead of 6.022 × 10^23) in calculating enzymatic rates. This error affected all plots in the original paper, and the corrected calculations show Vmax values approximately an order of magnitude lower than previously reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 clearly document a computational error in the original work. The error is straightforward (wrong exponent in Avogadro's number), and the magnitude of the correction (order of magnitude decrease in Vmax) is mathematically consistent with a 10-fold error in the constant. This is a transparent correction of a calculation error.

results.result: Correcting Avogadro's number shifts the optimal carboxysome permeability from kc = 6 × 10^-3 cm/s to kc = 10^-3 cm/s (a 6-fold decrease), makes the optimal permeability peak lower and broader, and causes carbonic anhydrase to saturate at lower HCO3− transport values. For high permeabilities (kc > 0.1 cm/s), CO2 concentration is an order of magnitude lower after correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23, C40-C42 describe consistent effects of the correction on optimal carboxysome permeability. The 6-fold shift in optimal permeability and order-of-magnitude changes in CO2 concentration at high permeabilities are mathematically consistent with the 10-fold correction in Avogadro's number. The phase space analysis in Figure 2 provides visual support for these quantitative changes.

results.result: After correction, decreasing the diffusion constant in the carboxysome has much less effect on the phase space plot, particularly at optimal or larger carboxysome permeability (kc ≥ 10^-3 cm/s), where the effect is very little.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 and C38 consistently describe reduced sensitivity to diffusion changes after the correction. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provides visual evidence comparing different diffusion constants. The finding that diffusion effects are minimal at optimal permeability is logically consistent with the corrected enzymatic rates.

results.result: The correction reduces the effect of facilitated CO2 uptake, with nearly no effect at the optimal permeability (kc = 10^-3 cm/s).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 describe reduced facilitated uptake effects after correction. Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the comparison between conditions with and without facilitated uptake (α = 0 vs α = 1 cm/s), supporting the claim that differences are minimal at optimal permeability.

results.result: Figure 3 plotted at the new optimal permeability shows very little change from the previous version, and the correction does not affect the conclusion that carbonic anhydrase organization within the carboxysome has no effect on resulting concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 and C37 indicate that certain conclusions remain unchanged despite the correction. The statement that Figure 3 shows little change when plotted at the new optimal permeability is reasonable, as the system is still at its optimum. Figure 3—figure supplement 1 supports the claim about carbonic anhydrase organization having no effect.

results.result: The correction does not affect the fundamental conclusion that an optimal carboxysome permeability exists or what causes it, but changes its absolute value.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 appropriately distinguishes between qualitative conclusions (existence of optimal permeability) and quantitative values (the specific optimal value). This is consistent with the correction affecting rate constants but not the underlying physical principles governing the system.

results.result: For Table 3, parameters were updated to reflect optimal conditions: flux changed from jc = 0.7 cm/s to jc = 0.6 cm/s and permeability from kc = 6 × 10^-3 cm/s to kc = 10^-3 cm/s, maintaining cytosolic HCO3− at 30 mM.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 document parameter updates for consistency with the corrected optimal permeability. The changes are modest and maintain the target cytosolic HCO3− concentration, which is appropriate for comparing corrected results under equivalent physiological conditions.

results.result: The conversion from picomoles/s to molecules/s used the incorrect Avogadro's number, resulting in a corrected flux of 2 × 10^8 molecules/s and a transporter density requirement of ~10^4 transporters/μm^2, which is about an order of magnitude larger than ATP synthase complexes on spinach thylakoid membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 and C91 describe the propagation of the Avogadro's number error to flux calculations. The order-of-magnitude increase in calculated transporter density (from 10^3 to 10^4 per μm^2) is mathematically consistent with the 10-fold correction. The comparison to ATP synthase provides biological context for evaluating the plausibility of the corrected value.

results.result: Correcting Avogadro's number lowers the calculated rates of carboxylation and oxygenation, resulting in only ~0.03% of concentrated inorganic carbon being fixed into 3-phosphoglycerate and many fewer 2-phosphoglycolate molecules produced than previously estimated.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 and C72 describe reduced fixation rates after correction. The very low percentage of carbon fixation (0.03%) compared to leakage (>99.9%) is concerning and suggests either the model has limitations or cyanobacteria operate under extreme energetic constraints. However, the calculations appear internally consistent with the corrected enzymatic rates.

results.result: Recalculated cell replication times are 7-21 hr for higher flux (Table 3) and 11-35 hr for lower flux (Table 4), both consistent with cyanobacteria division times, though the higher flux rate provides a better match.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 and C93-C94 present recalculated replication times that are now more biologically plausible than the original 1-2 hr estimate. The ranges overlap with known cyanobacteria division times, providing validation for the corrected model. The preference for the higher flux rate is appropriately stated as a better match rather than definitive.

results.result: After correction, CO2 scavenging is negligible compared to HCO3− uptake and CO2 uptake for all permeabilities shown, only contributing more than CO2 uptake when CO2 is a very small percentage of external carbon.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 and C95 consistently describe reduced CO2 scavenging effects after correction. Figure 5 provides visual evidence showing scavenging contributions are negligibly small across the parameter range tested. This represents a significant change from the original conclusions about scavenging importance.

results.result: With corrected Avogadro's number, CO2 concentration is significantly lower in all but the optimal permeability case, making the error rate drastically higher and the effect of optimal permeability on CO2 concentration much larger.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 describe increased importance of optimal permeability after correction. Figure 6 shows error rates for different cellular organizations, supporting the claim that non-optimal configurations result in much higher oxygenation error rates. This strengthens the biological significance of achieving optimal permeability.

results.result: Figure 2 uses three lines to demarcate key physiological boundaries: RuBisCO half-saturation (dark blue), 99% carboxylation efficiency at 260 μM O2 (light blue), and carbonic anhydrase saturation (red).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 describe the figure legend and interpretation of phase space boundaries. These are methodological descriptions that define how to read the phase space plots and are clearly supported by the figure caption and visual elements in Figure 2.
